questions.prompt: In a primary-replica (leader-follower) setup with asynchronous replication, what anomaly can a client observe?

options.text: The primary cannot accept writes while replicas lag
Writes to the primary are silently lost under normal operation
It may read its own write back as missing from a replica
Replicas reject all reads until fully caught up

questions.explanation: Replication lag means a read routed to a replica may predate the client's own write. Read-your-writes consistency is usually restored by pinning recent writers to the primary for a short window.

options.text: They are different names for the same technique
Sharding splits data across nodes; replication copies the same data to several nodes
Sharding applies only to caches, replication only to databases
Sharding copies all data to every node; replication splits it

questions.explanation: Sharding addresses capacity and write throughput by giving each node a disjoint subset. Replication addresses availability and read scaling by duplicating data. Large systems typically use both.

questions.prompt: A shard key is chosen that is highly skewed, such as country for a service dominated by one country. What is the consequence?

options.text: Queries return incorrect results
Replication lag becomes zero
One shard becomes a hotspot while others stay idle
The database refuses further writes

questions.explanation: Sharding only helps if load spreads evenly. A skewed key recreates the single-node bottleneck on one shard while wasting the rest — which is why high-cardinality, uniformly distributed keys are preferred.

questions.prompt: Which workload characteristic most strongly suggests a document or key-value store over a relational database?

options.text: Multi-row transactions spanning several entities
Complex multi-table joins and strict foreign key constraints
Ad hoc analytical queries over many dimensions
Simple lookups by key at very high volume with a flexible schema

questions.explanation: Key-value and document stores drop joins and rigid schemas in exchange for simple horizontal partitioning. Workloads that genuinely need joins or multi-entity transactions are better served relationally.

questions.prompt: Why does adding an index speed up reads but slow down writes?

options.text: Indexes force queries to scan more rows
Indexes are stored on slower disks than table data
Indexes lock the entire table during reads
The index must be updated on every insert, update and delete

questions.explanation: An index is a second structure the engine must keep consistent with the table. Every additional index therefore multiplies write cost and storage, which is why unused indexes are worth removing.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of connection pooling in front of a database?

options.text: It reuses established connections, avoiding setup cost and unbounded connection counts
It shards data across several databases
It encrypts traffic between application and database
It caches query results in the application

questions.explanation: Opening a connection costs a round trip and server memory. A pool amortises that cost and, just as importantly, caps concurrent connections so a traffic spike cannot exhaust the database.

questions.prompt: In a read-heavy system, what is the most common reason to add read replicas rather than a cache?

options.text: Replicas serve arbitrary queries, whereas a cache serves only precomputed keys
Replicas are always strongly consistent with the primary
Replicas remove the need for indexes
Replicas reduce write latency

questions.explanation: A cache only helps for lookups you can key in advance. Replicas run the full query engine, so ad hoc and analytical reads can be offloaded without predicting access patterns.

questions.prompt: What does denormalising a schema trade away?

options.text: Read speed, in exchange for smaller storage
The ability to index any column
Write simplicity and update consistency, in exchange for faster reads
Support for transactions entirely

questions.explanation: Duplicating data avoids joins at read time, but every copy must now be updated together or they drift apart. It is the same redundancy that normalisation exists to remove, accepted deliberately.

questions.prompt: What problem does a write-ahead log solve in a database?

options.text: It allows committed changes to survive a crash by recording intent before applying it
It compresses data before writing it to disk
It distributes writes across shards
It removes the need for indexes on write-heavy tables

questions.explanation: Appending to a log is sequential and fast, and it means recovery can replay or undo whatever was in flight. It is also the natural stream to ship to replicas, which is how replication is usually built.

questions.prompt: A service must support both high-volume transactional writes and heavy analytical queries. What is the usual architectural response?

options.text: Drop all indexes to speed up the analytical queries
Separate them, replicating transactional data into an analytical store
Shard by timestamp so old data is deleted automatically
Run both workloads on the same primary database instance

questions.explanation: The two workloads want opposite things — row-oriented short transactions versus column-oriented full scans. Keeping them on one instance means long analytical queries starve the transactional path.
